newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: E.Europe states weigh life inside and outside EU.
newsitem.headline: E.Europe states weigh life inside and outside EU.

text.p: Central and Eastern European states, absorbing news that the European Commission would recommend entry talks with only five of them, knuckled down on Friday to economic realities inside and outside the bloc.
Reactions from EU hopefuls to news the Commission would favour the Czech Republic, Poland, Hungary, Estonia, Slovenia and Cyprus ranged from elation to bitter disappointment.

"I hope that the member countries of the European Union...will not turn their backs on Slovakia," Slovak President Michal Kovac told Reuters in a first reaction during the Second Central and Eastern European Economic Summit.
His remarks were in stark contrast to the joy of Estonian Prime Minister Mart Siiman. "We are extremely happy about this..Our expectations are becoming reality."

Central bankers swiftly focused their minds on the economic impacts of the EU's expansion and the likely effects on them of Europe's planned single currency, which is due for launch on January 1, 1999.
For the Czech Republic, Poland, Hungary, Estonia and Slovenia the euro's successful introduction is the final hurdle between them and the start of EU entry negotiations.
"Central European countries are interested in a timely introduction of the euro as a prerequisite for starting enlargement talks," said Gyorgy Suranyi, president of the National Bank of Hungary.

Former communist states that appeared to have missed out on the first wave of the bloc's eastward expansion fixed their sights on a more distant goal -- the timing of their integration into the EU and survival outside.

Analysts have warned that a decision to limit the number of EU entrants, coming hot on the heels of NATO's decision to invite just three Central and East Europen states, may create a new order of winners and losers in the region.
"Latvia is strongly committed to becoming a full member of the European Union," Latvian central bank head Einars Repse told delegates.
He played down doomsday scenarios of a strong euro area that would draw investment away from the transition economies while stemming trade flows between Eastern and Western Europe.

"We do not need any serious modifications of our policies (to cope with the euro). The only possible exchange rate policy change will be switching our peg from the SDR (Special Drawing Rights) to the euro," Repse said.

"There is a danger that the EMU (European economic and monetary union) bloc will suddenly become a large and closed economic region. This could in turn lead to a trade fortress in Europe," said one economist.
Hungary, the Czech Republic and Poland said they were well prepared to cope with tougher competition inside the European Union and saw their economies well on the road to integration.
"I believe the Czech economy will become more and more financially integrated in the EU, regardless of whether it is a member of the Union or not," said Czech central banker Josef Tosovsky.
